title: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth

topics.title: People as wealth and the idea of distribution

learn.hook: India's biggest resource isn't coal or iron — it's 140 crore people. Geography starts by asking where they live.
points: The people of a country are its real wealth: they use its resources and decide its policies; a country is ultimately known by its people.
World population has crossed 8 billion (the UN marked this in November 2022), after growing slowly for most of history and very fast in the last few centuries.
Geographers study population under four heads: distribution, density, growth and composition.
Distribution means the way people are spaced over the earth's surface — some areas are crowded, others nearly empty.

example.q: A teacher asks: 'Name the four aspects in which population is studied, and define the first one.'
steps: The four aspects are distribution, density, growth and composition.
Distribution is the first.
It refers to the way people are spaced over the earth's surface.
example.answer: Distribution, density, growth, composition; distribution = spacing of people over the earth's surface

learn.reallife: India's demographic dividend — a huge young workforce powering IT services in Bengaluru and factories in Tamil Nadu — shows why people are called a nation's real wealth.

items.text: Geographers study population under distribution, density, growth and ___.
The way people are spaced over the earth's surface is called population ___.

games.title: Real wealth?
items: The people of a country are called its real wealth.
They use resources and make policies.
Population is evenly spread over the earth's surface.
Population growth was always fast throughout history.
It was slow for a long time and fast only recently.
Composition is one of the aspects in which population is studied.

quiz.q: Why are the people of a country called its real wealth?
options: They own all the minerals personally
They use its resources and make its policies
quiz.explain: People turn resources into wealth and shape decisions, so they are the real wealth.
steps: Asked: why people are a country's real wealth.
Lesson: people use the country's resources and decide its policies.
So the answer is that they use its resources and make its policies.
Answer: They use its resources and make its policies
quiz.mistake: Thinks wealth means only money or minerals

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four aspects in which population is usually studied?
quiz.explain: Population is studied by distribution, density, growth and composition. Altitude is a physical feature.
steps: The four aspects: distribution, density, growth and composition.
Altitude is not in the list — it is a physical feature of land.
So altitude is the answer.
Answer: Altitude
quiz.mistake: Adds a physical feature to the list

quiz.q: 'The way people are spaced over the earth's surface' defines:
quiz.explain: Distribution is about pattern of spacing; density is a ratio of people to area.
steps: Asked: the term for how people are spaced over the earth's surface.
Lesson: that is distribution.
Density is a ratio (people per sq km), so it does not fit the definition.
Answer: Distribution of population
quiz.mistake: Confuses distribution with density

quiz.q: World population crossed which mark in November 2022, according to the UN?
quiz.explain: The UN announced the world reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022.
steps: Asked: the mark crossed in November 2022.
Lesson: the UN marked world population crossing 8 billion then.
So the answer is 8 billion.
Answer: 8 billion
quiz.mistake: Uses an outdated figure

quiz.q: Which statement about historical world population growth is correct?
options: It has been rapid at a constant rate since prehistoric times
It was slow for a long time and became very rapid in recent centuries
It has fallen continuously since the 1800s
quiz.explain: Growth was slow in early periods and speeded up after the Industrial Revolution.
steps: Asked: the correct trend of growth over history.
Lesson: growth was slow for most of history and very fast in recent centuries.
So 'slow for a long time, then very rapid' is correct.
Answer: It was slow for a long time and became very rapid in recent centuries
quiz.mistake: Assumes constant fast growth

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A country is ultimately known by its people. Reason (R): People use the country's resources and decide its policies.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; because people are the users of resources and makers of policy, a country is identified by them.
steps: Check A: a country is known by its people — true.
Check R: people use resources and decide policies — true.
Because people run the country, it is identified by them, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks R is unrelated to A

quiz.q: Which pair is correct for the study of population?
options: Distribution — people per unit area; Density — spacing of people
Distribution — spacing of people; Density — people per unit area
Growth — sex ratio; Composition — birth rate
quiz.explain: Distribution = pattern of spacing; density = ratio of people to land area.
steps: Distribution = spacing of people over the earth's surface.
Density = people per unit area.
Only the option 'Distribution — spacing; Density — people per unit area' matches.
Answer: Distribution — spacing of people; Density — people per unit area
quiz.mistake: Swaps the two definitions

quiz.q: A map shows dots crowded along the Ganga valley and few dots in the Thar desert. This map mainly shows population:
quiz.explain: A dot map showing where people live shows distribution.
steps: The map shows where people are crowded (Ganga valley) and where few live (Thar).
Showing where people live is population distribution.
It shows no change over time, so it is not growth.
Answer: Distribution
quiz.mistake: Thinks any population map shows growth

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does population distribution mean, and in what other ways do geographers study population?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Distribution, density, growth and composition — four lenses to look at people!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the other aspects besides distribution?

revise.summary: A country's people are its real wealth because they use its resources and make its policies. World population crossed 8 billion in November 2022, and geographers study it by distribution, density, growth and composition.
focus: The four aspects: distribution, density, growth and composition
Telling distribution (spacing of people) from density (people per unit area)
Why people are called the real wealth of a country
remember: Population is studied by distribution, density, growth and composition
Distribution = the way people are spaced over the earth's surface
World population crossed 8 billion in November 2022 (UN)
traps: Don't swap distribution and density — density is a ratio of people to area
Don't think world population always grew fast — it was slow for most of history

learn.hook: Nine out of ten people on Earth squeeze into just one-tenth of its land. Where are they all?
points: About 90 per cent of the world's population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area.
The 10 most populous countries contribute about 60 per cent of world population; 6 of these 10 are in Asia.
India and China together hold over a third of humanity; India became the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate).
On a world map, densely populated belts lie in East, South and South-east Asia, north-western Europe and north-eastern USA; sparse areas lie near the poles, in deserts and in equatorial rainforests.

example.q: If world population is 8 billion, about how many people live on 10 per cent of the land?
steps: About 90% of people live on 10% of land.
90% of 8 billion = 0.9 × 8 = 7.2 billion.

learn.reallife: India's population is about 18 per cent of the world but on only about 2.4 per cent of world land — a classic example of uneven distribution.

games.title: Distribution facts
items: About 90% of the world's population lives in about 10% of its land area.
Of the 10 most populous countries, 6 are in Asia.
The 10 most populous countries hold about 25% of world population.
Antarctica is one of the densely populated regions.

quiz.q: About what share of the world's population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area?
quiz.explain: Population is very unevenly spread: about 90% live on about 10% of land.
steps: Asked: share of people living on about 10% of land.
Lesson: about 90% of the world's population lives on about 10% of its land.
So the answer is 90%; 60% is the top-10 countries' share.
Answer: 90%
quiz.mistake: Confuses this with the 60% share of the top 10 countries

quiz.q: The 10 most populous countries together contribute about what share of world population?
quiz.explain: NCERT notes the top 10 countries contribute about 60%.
steps: Asked: share of world population in the 10 most populous countries.
Lesson: about 60%.
90% is the land-concentration figure, so it is wrong here.
Answer: 60%
quiz.mistake: Picks the 90% figure meant for land concentration

quiz.q: How many of the 10 most populous countries are located in Asia?
quiz.explain: Six of the ten most populous countries are in Asia.
steps: Asked: how many of the top 10 countries are in Asia.
Lesson: 6 of the 10 most populous countries are in Asia.
So the answer is 6.
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Underestimates Asia's share

quiz.q: If the world has 8 billion people, roughly how many billion people live in the 10 most populous countries (about 60%)?
quiz.explain: 60% of 8 billion = 0.6 × 8 = 4.8 billion.
steps: 0.6 × 8 = 4.8 billion
Answer: 4.8
quiz.mistake: Uses 90% instead of 60%

quiz.q: On a world population map, which area would appear sparsely populated?
quiz.explain: Hot deserts like the Sahara have very few people.
steps: Sparse areas: near the poles, hot and cold deserts, equatorial rainforests.
The interior of the Sahara is a hot desert.
Ganga plains, north-eastern USA and eastern China are dense belts.
Answer: Interior of the Sahara
quiz.mistake: Mixes dense and sparse areas

quiz.q: Which continent has the largest number of the world's most populous countries?
quiz.explain: Asia has 6 of the top 10.
steps: Lesson: 6 of the 10 most populous countries are in Asia.
No other continent has as many.
So the answer is Asia.
Answer: Asia
quiz.mistake: Thinks Africa leads because of high growth rates

quiz.q: Assertion (A): World population distribution is highly uneven. Reason (R): About 90 per cent of people live in about 10 per cent of the land area.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, and R is the data that shows A.
steps: Check A: distribution is highly uneven — true.
Check R: about 90% live on about 10% of land — true.
That statistic is the evidence of unevenness, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the statistic and the unevenness are unrelated

quiz.q: Which country became the world's most populous in 2023, according to UN estimates?
quiz.explain: UN estimates showed India overtaking China in 2023.
steps: Asked: country that became most populous in 2023.
Lesson: UN estimates show India overtook China in 2023.
So the answer is India.
Answer: India
quiz.mistake: Uses an outdated fact

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is the world's population spread evenly? Give me some numbers.'
teach.praise: Chirp! 90% of people on 10% of land — that's really crowded!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you give the 90% / 10% fact, and say where most people live?

revise.summary: World population is very unevenly spread: about 90% of people live on about 10% of the land. The 10 most populous countries hold about 60% of people, 6 of them in Asia, and India became the most populous country in 2023.
focus: The 90% on 10% of land figure and the 60% top-10 figure
Dense belts vs sparse areas on a world map
Asia's share of the most populous countries
remember: About 90% of people live on about 10% of the land
10 most populous countries ≈ 60% of world population; 6 of the 10 are in Asia
India became the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate)
traps: Don't mix the 90% (land concentration) with the 60% (top 10 countries)
Sparse areas are near the poles, in deserts and in equatorial rainforests — not north-eastern USA

learn.hook: Bihar packs over 1,100 people into each square kilometre; Arunachal Pradesh, about 17. Same country, very different crowding!
points: Density of population = number of people ÷ area of land; expressed as persons per sq km.
Example: a region of 100 sq km with 1,50,000 people has density 1,50,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500 persons per sq km.
Densely populated regions: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, and South, South-east and East Asia.
Sparsely populated regions: areas near the North and South Poles, hot and cold deserts, and high rainfall zones near the equator.
Medium density regions: western China, southern India, Norway and Sweden.

example.q: District A has 24,00,000 people on 1,200 sq km. District B has 9,00,000 people on 300 sq km. Which is denser?
steps: Density B = 9,00,000 ÷ 300 = 3,000 per sq km.
B is denser even though it has fewer people.

learn.reallife: Census 2011 recorded India's density as 382 persons per sq km — Delhi topped among states/UTs, while Arunachal Pradesh was the lowest.

items.q: A density of 500 on 20 sq km means how many people?

quiz.q: Density of population is expressed as:
quiz.explain: Density is a ratio of people to land area, so the unit is persons per sq km.
steps: Asked: the unit of density.
Density = people ÷ land area.
So it is expressed as persons per sq km, not per year.
Answer: Persons per sq km
quiz.mistake: Confuses density with growth rate or birth rate

quiz.q: A region has an area of 100 sq km and a population of 1,50,000. What is its density (persons per sq km)?
quiz.explain: Density = 1,50,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500 persons per sq km.
steps: Density = population ÷ area
1,50,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500 persons per sq km
Answer: 1,500
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing, or misplaces zeros

quiz.q: A taluka of 250 sq km has a density of 600 persons per sq km. What is its population?
quiz.explain: Population = density × area = 600 × 250 = 1,50,000.
steps: Population = density × area
Answer: 1,50,000
quiz.mistake: Divides or adds instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Which of these is a medium density region of the world?
quiz.explain: NCERT lists western China, southern India, Norway and Sweden as medium density.
steps: Lesson: medium density regions are western China, southern India, Norway and Sweden.
North-eastern USA and Bangladesh are dense; polar regions are sparse.
So the answer is Norway and Sweden.
Answer: Norway and Sweden
quiz.mistake: Picks a high-density region

quiz.q: Which is NOT a sparsely populated region?
options: High rainfall zones near the equator
quiz.explain: North-western Europe is densely populated; the others are sparse.
steps: Sparse: near the poles, cold and hot deserts, equatorial high rainfall zones.
North-western Europe is listed as densely populated.
So north-western Europe is NOT sparse.
Answer: North-western Europe
quiz.mistake: Thinks all cold places are sparse, including Europe

quiz.q: Town P: 6,00,000 people on 200 sq km. Town Q: 8,00,000 people on 400 sq km. By how many persons per sq km is P's density greater than Q's?
quiz.explain: P = 3,000 and Q = 2,000 persons per sq km, so P is denser by 1,000.
steps: Answer: 1,000
quiz.mistake: Compares total populations instead of densities

quiz.q: Assertion (A): High rainfall zones near the equator are sparsely populated. Reason (R): Dense forests, heat and humidity make settlement and farming difficult there.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the harsh conditions of equatorial rainforests explain the sparse population.
steps: Check A: equatorial high rainfall zones are sparse — true.
Check R: dense forest, heat and humidity make settling and farming hard — true.
Those harsh conditions cause the low population, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks heavy rain always means dense farming population

quiz.q: Which region is among the most densely populated in the world?
quiz.explain: South, South-east and East Asia are among the most densely populated regions.
steps: Dense regions: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, South, South-east and East Asia.
Central Australia, Siberia and Greenland are large but nearly empty.
So South Asia is the answer.
Answer: South Asia
quiz.mistake: Picks a large but empty region

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do you calculate population density, and where in the world is it high or low?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! People divided by area — and Asia is packed while the poles are empty!
teach.nudge: Nice! Give the formula for density and name one dense and one sparse region.

revise.summary: Density of population = number of people ÷ area, in persons per sq km. Dense regions include north-eastern USA, north-western Europe and South, South-east and East Asia; sparse regions are polar areas, deserts and equatorial rainforests.
focus: Calculating density, and population from density × area
Classifying regions as dense, medium or sparse
Comparing densities rather than total populations
remember: Density = population ÷ area (persons per sq km)
Dense: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, South, South-east and East Asia
Medium: western China, southern India, Norway, Sweden
Sparse: near the poles, hot and cold deserts, high rainfall zones near the equator
traps: Don't multiply population by area to get density — divide
A place with more people is not always denser; compare people per sq km

learn.hook: Why did the great civilisations grow along the Nile, the Indus and the Hwang He? Follow the water.
points: Availability of water: people prefer areas where fresh water is easily available; river valleys are among the most densely populated areas.
Landforms: people prefer flat plains and gentle slopes, which suit farming, roads and industry. Ganga plains are densely populated; mountains like the Andes, Alps and Himalayas are sparse.
Climate: extreme climates such as very hot or cold deserts are uncomfortable; areas with a comfortable climate with little seasonal variation, like Mediterranean regions, attract people.
Soils: fertile loamy soils support intensive agriculture, so plains of the Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang (in China) are densely populated.

example.q: Explain why the Ganga plains are far more crowded than Ladakh.
steps: Water: perennial Ganga and tributaries vs scarce water in Ladakh.
Landform: flat plain vs high mountains.
Climate and soil: moderate climate and fertile alluvium vs cold desert and thin soils.
example.answer: Water, flat land, fertile soil and moderate climate make the Ganga plains densely populated

learn.reallife: The Indo-Gangetic plain supports some of the world's highest rural densities thanks to rivers, alluvial soil and canal irrigation.

games.title: Factor and example
pairs: Fertile loamy plains of the Nile and Chang Jiang

games.title: Geography decides
items: Mountains like the Alps and Andes are densely populated.
Fertile loamy soils support intensive agriculture.
That is why alluvial river plains are crowded.
Hot and cold deserts have extreme climates that discourage settlement.
Discomfort and difficulty of farming keep numbers low.
River valleys are among the least populated parts of the world.
They are among the most densely populated.
Mediterranean regions attracted people due to their pleasant climate.

quiz.q: Which geographical factor explains why river valleys are among the most densely populated areas?
quiz.explain: Fresh water for drinking, farming and transport draws people to river valleys.
steps: Asked: why river valleys are densely populated.
Lesson: people prefer areas where fresh water is easily available.
So the factor is availability of water.
Answer: Availability of water
quiz.mistake: Picks an economic or social factor

quiz.q: Why are the Himalayas, Andes and Alps sparsely populated?
options: Rugged landforms make farming, transport and settlement difficult
quiz.explain: Steep slopes and harsh terrain discourage settlement.
steps: Asked: why the Himalayas, Andes and Alps are sparse.
Lesson: people prefer flat land; rugged mountains make farming, transport and settlement hard.
So the answer is rugged landforms.
Answer: Rugged landforms make farming, transport and settlement difficult
quiz.mistake: Thinks mountains lack water

quiz.q: Which plains are cited for fertile loamy soils and dense population?
options: Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang
quiz.explain: These alluvial river plains support intensive farming.
steps: Asked: plains with fertile loamy soils and dense population.
Lesson: Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang plains.
Sahara, Thar and tundra are sparse, so they are wrong.
Answer: Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang
quiz.mistake: Picks deserts or tundra

quiz.q: Which climate type has historically attracted people due to its pleasantness?
quiz.explain: The comfortable Mediterranean climate attracted people from early times.
steps: Asked: climate that attracted people for its pleasantness.
Lesson: comfortable climates with little seasonal change, like the Mediterranean, attract people.
So the answer is Mediterranean.
Answer: Mediterranean
quiz.mistake: Thinks hot deserts are attractive due to sunshine

quiz.q: A region is flat, has fertile alluvium and a perennial river, but is in a cold desert. Which factor would most limit its population?
quiz.explain: All other factors are favourable; the extreme cold climate is the limiting factor.
steps: Check each factor: flat land ✓, fertile alluvium ✓, perennial river ✓.
Only the climate (cold desert) is unfavourable.
So climate is the limiting factor.
Answer: Climate
quiz.mistake: Ignores the cold desert clue

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Plains are preferred for human settlement. Reason (R): They are suitable for agriculture, construction of roads and industries.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the ease of farming and building on flat land explains the preference.
steps: Check A: plains are preferred for settlement — true.
Check R: they suit agriculture, roads and industries — true.
That ease of use is why people prefer plains, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect ease of use to settlement

quiz.q: Which of these is a geographical (not economic or social) factor of population distribution?
quiz.explain: Water, landforms, climate and soils are geographical factors.
steps: Geographical factors: water, landforms, climate, soils.
Urbanisation and industrialisation are economic; religious importance is cultural.
So the answer is soils.
Answer: Soils
quiz.mistake: Treats urbanisation as a geographical factor

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly explains low population in the Thar desert?
quiz.explain: The Thar has a hot, dry climate and scarce water.
steps: The Thar is a hot desert.
Its limits are an extreme climate and scarce water.
Rugged mountains and dense forests describe other regions, not the Thar.
Answer: Extreme climate and scarce water
quiz.mistake: Applies mountain or rainforest reasons to a desert

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What natural factors decide where people live?' Name and explain at least three.
teach.praise: Chirp! Water, land, climate and soil — nature's four magnets!
teach.nudge: Good! You missed one — think about water, landforms, climate and soils.

revise.summary: Geographical factors shape where people live: fresh water, flat plains, a comfortable climate and fertile soils attract people, so river valleys and plains like the Ganga are crowded, while mountains, deserts and polar areas are sparse.
focus: The four geographical factors: water, landforms, climate, soils
Using factors to explain dense vs sparse areas
Finding the limiting factor in a case
remember: River valleys are among the most densely populated areas because of fresh water
Plains and gentle slopes suit farming, roads and industry; mountains (Andes, Alps, Himalayas) are sparse
Fertile loamy soils: plains of the Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang are dense
traps: Urbanisation and industrialisation are economic factors, not geographical
Don't say mountains are empty for lack of water — rugged terrain is the reason

learn.hook: Jamshedpur grew from a forest village to a steel city in a few decades. What pulled people there?
points: Minerals: areas with mineral deposits attract industries, and mining and industrial activity create jobs; e.g. the Katanga-Zambia copper belt in Africa.
Urbanisation: cities offer better civic amenities, employment, education, medical facilities and transport, so they attract rural-urban migrants and grow large.
Industrialisation: industrial belts provide jobs for factory workers and also transport operators, shopkeepers, bank staff, doctors and teachers; e.g. Kobe-Osaka region of Japan.

Social and cultural factors: places of religious or cultural significance attract people (Varanasi, Jerusalem, Vatican City); social and political unrest pushes people out; governments sometimes offer incentives to settle sparse areas.

example.q: Classify: (i) Jharia coalfield town grows; (ii) pilgrims settle in Varanasi; (iii) people leave a conflict-hit region; (iv) Gurugram's offices draw graduates.
steps: (i) Minerals → economic.
(ii) Religious significance → social/cultural.
(iii) Unrest → social/political push.
(iv) Urban jobs and amenities → economic (urbanisation).

learn.reallife: Migrants from Bihar and UP to Mumbai, Surat and Delhi follow jobs created by industrialisation and urbanisation.

quiz.q: The Kobe-Osaka region of Japan is densely populated mainly due to:
quiz.explain: NCERT cites Kobe-Osaka as an industrial belt that attracts large numbers of people.
steps: Asked: why the Kobe-Osaka region is dense.
Lesson: it is cited as an industrial belt that attracts many people.
So the answer is industrialisation.
Answer: Industrialisation
quiz.mistake: Picks a geographical factor

quiz.q: Which is an example of a mineral-rich area attracting population?
quiz.explain: Mining and associated industry in the copper belt attract workers.
steps: Asked: a mineral-rich area that attracts population.
Lesson: the Katanga-Zambia copper belt in Africa.
Vatican City is a religious centre, so it is wrong.
Answer: Katanga-Zambia copper belt
quiz.mistake: Confuses a religious centre with a mining area

quiz.q: Varanasi, Jerusalem and Vatican City attract people mainly because of:
quiz.explain: These are religious and cultural centres.
steps: Asked: why Varanasi, Jerusalem and Vatican City attract people.
Lesson: they are places of religious or cultural significance.
So the answer is religious or cultural significance.
Answer: Religious or cultural significance
quiz.mistake: Assumes all big draws are economic

quiz.q: Industrial belts attract not only factory workers but also:
options: Transport operators, shopkeepers, bank employees, doctors and teachers
quiz.explain: Industries generate many service jobs too.
steps: Asked: who else industrial belts attract.
Lesson: transport operators, shopkeepers, bank staff, doctors and teachers.
So industries create many service jobs, not just factory ones.
Answer: Transport operators, shopkeepers, bank employees, doctors and teachers
quiz.mistake: Thinks industries employ only factory hands

quiz.q: Social and political unrest in a region usually leads to:
options: People moving out of the region
quiz.explain: Unrest is a push factor causing outmigration.
steps: Asked: the effect of social and political unrest.
Lesson: unrest pushes people out of a region.
So the answer is people moving out.
Answer: People moving out of the region
quiz.mistake: Thinks unrest has no effect on population

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Cities attract large numbers of rural migrants. Reason (R): Cities offer better civic amenities, employment, education and medical facilities.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; these attractions explain the rural-urban migration.
steps: Check A: cities attract many rural migrants — true.
Check R: cities offer better amenities, jobs, education and medical care — true.
These attractions cause the migration, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats A and R as separate facts

quiz.q: Which of these is an economic factor influencing population distribution?
quiz.explain: Minerals, urbanisation and industrialisation are economic factors.
steps: Economic factors: minerals, urbanisation, industrialisation.
Climate and landforms are geographical; religious significance is cultural.
So the answer is urbanisation.
Answer: Urbanisation
quiz.mistake: Treats climate as economic

quiz.q: A new steel plant opens near an iron ore mine in a forested area. Over 20 years the area's population will most likely:
options: Increase, as jobs attract workers and service providers
quiz.explain: Mining and industry create jobs, attracting people — as in Jamshedpur or Bhilai.
steps: A steel plant near an iron ore mine creates jobs.
Jobs attract workers and service providers, as in Jamshedpur.
So the population will most likely increase.
Answer: Increase, as jobs attract workers and service providers
quiz.mistake: Ignores the pull of employment

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Apart from nature, what else pulls people to a place or pushes them away?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Mines, cities, factories and sacred places — people follow them all!
teach.nudge: Good! Mention economic factors like minerals and industry, and social or cultural ones too.

revise.summary: Economic factors (minerals, urbanisation, industrialisation) and social-cultural factors (religious centres, unrest, government incentives) also shape population distribution. Jobs and amenities pull people in; unrest pushes them out.

Classifying a case as economic or social-cultural
How industrial belts create service jobs too
remember: Economic factors: minerals, urbanisation, industrialisation
Katanga-Zambia copper belt = minerals; Kobe-Osaka region of Japan = industrialisation
Religious/cultural centres: Varanasi, Jerusalem, Vatican City; social and political unrest pushes people out
traps: Don't treat climate or landforms as economic factors
Industries do not employ only factory workers — they also draw shopkeepers, bank staff, doctors and teachers

learn.hook: India added about 18 crore people between Census 2001 and 2011. How do geographers measure change on that scale?
points: Population growth (population change) is the change in the number of inhabitants of a territory over a period of time; it may be positive or negative.
Growth of population: change between two points of time in absolute numbers = later population − earlier population.
Growth rate of population: the change expressed as a percentage = (change ÷ earlier population) × 100.
Growth rate lets us compare places of very different sizes fairly.

example.q: A town had 50,000 people in 2011 and 60,000 in 2021. Find the growth and the growth rate.

learn.reallife: Census 2011 showed India's decadal growth rate as 17.7% for 2001–2011, the lowest decadal growth recorded after Independence.

games.title: Growth or rate?
items: Growth of population is expressed in absolute numbers.
It is the actual difference in numbers.
Growth rate is expressed as a percentage.
Population change can never be negative.
It is negative when population falls.
Growth rate is calculated by dividing the change by the later population.

quiz.q: A district's population rose from 8,00,000 in 2011 to 9,20,000 in 2021. What is the growth of population?
quiz.explain: Growth in absolute numbers = 9,20,000 − 8,00,000 = 1,20,000.
steps: Growth = later − earlier
Answer: 1,20,000
quiz.mistake: Adds the two figures or gives the rate instead

quiz.q: For the same district (8,00,000 → 9,20,000), what is the growth rate?
steps: Answer: 15%
quiz.mistake: Divides by the later population (9,20,000), giving 13.04%

quiz.q: A hill town shrank from 25,000 to 20,000 people. What is its growth rate?
steps: Answer: −20%
quiz.mistake: Divides by 20,000 (giving −25%) or drops the minus sign

quiz.q: The difference between population figures at two points of time, in absolute numbers, is called:
quiz.explain: Growth = absolute change; growth rate = percentage change.
steps: Asked: the term for the absolute difference between two population figures.
Lesson: growth of population = change in absolute numbers.
Growth rate is the same change as a percentage, so it is wrong.
Answer: Growth of population
quiz.mistake: Confuses growth with growth rate

quiz.q: Population change expressed as a percentage is called:
quiz.explain: The growth rate expresses change in per cent.
steps: Asked: the term for change expressed as a percentage.
Lesson: growth rate = (change ÷ earlier population) × 100.
So the answer is growth rate of population.
Answer: Growth rate of population
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'growth' and 'growth rate' are the same

quiz.q: Village A grew from 1,000 to 1,200; city B from 10,00,000 to 11,00,000. Which grew at a faster rate?
options: Both grew at the same rate
City B, because it added more people
quiz.explain: A: 200 ÷ 1,000 = 20%; B: 1,00,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = 10%. The rate, not the absolute number, decides.
steps: 20% > 10%, so village A grew at the faster rate
Answer: Village A (20% vs 10%)
quiz.mistake: Thinks larger absolute addition means faster growth

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Growth rate is more useful than absolute growth for comparing places. Reason (R): Growth rate expresses change relative to the base population.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; because the rate is relative to the base, it allows fair comparison of places of different sizes.
steps: Check A: growth rate compares places better than absolute growth — true.
Check R: growth rate is relative to the base population — true.
Being relative to the base is what makes comparison fair, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks absolute numbers compare fairly

quiz.q: A state's population was 5 crore in 2011. With a growth rate of 12% by 2021, what would its 2021 population be (in crore)?
quiz.explain: New population = 5 × 1.12 = 5.6 crore.
steps: Increase = 12% of 5 crore = 0.12 × 5 = 0.6 crore
New = 5 + 0.6 = 5.6 crore
Answer: 5.6
quiz.mistake: Adds 12 as a decimal (5.12) or gives only the increase

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the difference between growth of population and growth rate? How do I calculate each?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Subtract for growth, divide by the earlier figure and ×100 for growth rate. Got it!
teach.nudge: Close! Say how growth rate is calculated — what do you divide by, and what do you multiply by?

revise.summary: Population growth is the change in the number of people between two points of time. Growth = later − earlier population; growth rate = (change ÷ earlier population) × 100, which lets us compare places of different sizes fairly.

Dividing by the earlier (base) population

Growth rate = (change ÷ earlier population) × 100

A bigger absolute increase does not mean a faster growth rate

topics.title: Natural growth, actual growth, positive and negative growth

learn.hook: Kerala has low birth rates, yet its villages fill with new houses built by Gulf migrants. Births alone don't tell the whole story.
points: Natural growth of population = births − deaths in a region between two points of time.
Actual growth of population = births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration.
Positive growth: when births exceed deaths between two points of time, or when people from other countries migrate in permanently.
Negative growth: when the population decreases between two points of time — births fall below deaths or people emigrate.

example.q: A city records 30,000 births, 10,000 deaths, 15,000 in-migrants and 5,000 out-migrants in a year. Find natural and actual growth.

learn.reallife: Several countries such as Japan and some in eastern Europe have recorded negative population growth as deaths outnumber births.

items.q: Births 500, deaths 200, in 100, out 50: actual growth?
Births 1000, deaths 400, in 0, out 700: actual growth?
Births 250, deaths 100, in 300, out 100: actual growth?

games.title: Positive or negative?
items: Deaths exceed births with no migration

quiz.q: Natural growth of population is the difference between:
quiz.explain: Natural growth considers only births and deaths.
steps: Asked: what natural growth compares.
Lesson: natural growth = births − deaths.
Migration is not included, so the answer is births and deaths.
Answer: Births and deaths
quiz.mistake: Includes migration in natural growth

quiz.q: Which formula gives the actual growth of population?
quiz.explain: Actual growth adds net migration to natural growth.
steps: Asked: formula for actual growth.
Lesson: actual growth = Births − Deaths + In-migration − Out-migration.
'Births − Deaths' alone is natural growth.
Answer: Births − Deaths + In-migration − Out-migration
quiz.mistake: Uses the natural growth formula

quiz.q: A region has 12,000 births, 4,000 deaths, 3,000 in-migrants and 9,000 out-migrants. What is its actual growth?
steps: Answer: 2,000
quiz.mistake: Stops at natural growth (8,000) or mixes signs of migration

quiz.q: For the same region (12,000 births, 4,000 deaths), what is the natural growth?
steps: Given: births = 12,000, deaths = 4,000.
Natural growth = Births − Deaths.
Answer: 8,000
quiz.mistake: Includes migration

quiz.q: When does a country show negative growth of population?
options: When population decreases between two points of time
quiz.explain: Negative growth means the number of people falls.
steps: Asked: when growth is negative.
Lesson: negative growth = population decreases between two points of time.
High density has nothing to do with it.
Answer: When population decreases between two points of time
quiz.mistake: Links negative growth to high density

quiz.q: Which situation can produce positive growth even if births equal deaths?
quiz.explain: With natural growth zero, net in-migration still adds people.
steps: If births = deaths, natural growth is zero.
Lesson: positive growth also occurs when people migrate in permanently from other countries.
So permanent immigration can still give positive growth.
Answer: Permanent immigration from other countries
quiz.mistake: Thinks only births add people

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A region can have positive natural growth but negative actual growth. Reason (R): Out-migration from the region may exceed natural increase plus in-migration.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; heavy out-migration can outweigh natural increase, making actual growth negative.
steps: Check A: natural growth can be positive while actual growth is negative — true.
Check R: out-migration may exceed natural increase plus in-migration — true.
That heavy out-migration is what turns the total negative, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Assumes natural and actual growth always share the same sign

quiz.q: A hill district has 2,000 births, 1,500 deaths, 200 in-migrants and 1,200 out-migrants. Its actual growth is:
quiz.explain: 2,000 − 1,500 + 200 − 1,200 = −500, so the district shrinks despite natural growth of +500.
steps: Net migration = 200 − 1,200 = −1,000
Answer: −500
quiz.mistake: Reports only natural growth (+500)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the difference between natural growth and actual growth? When is growth negative?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Natural = births minus deaths; actual adds migration; negative means fewer people!
teach.nudge: Good! Remember to include migration in actual growth, and say when growth is negative.

revise.summary: Natural growth = births − deaths. Actual growth = births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration. Growth is positive when population rises (more births or permanent immigration) and negative when it falls.

Positive vs negative growth
How migration can make actual growth differ from natural growth

Actual growth = Births − Deaths + In-migration − Out-migration
Negative growth: population decreases between two points of time

Natural growth and actual growth need not have the same sign

topics.title: Births and deaths: CBR, CDR and mortality

learn.hook: Every year the Sample Registration System tells India how many babies were born per 1,000 people. That single number shapes school and hospital budgets.
points: The three components of population change are births, deaths and migration.
Crude Birth Rate (CBR) = number of live births in a year per thousand of population: CBR = (Bi ÷ P) × 1000, where Bi = live births in the year and P = mid-year population.
Crude Death Rate (CDR) = number of deaths in a year per thousand of population: CDR = (D ÷ P) × 1000.
Mortality is affected by the region's demographic structure, social advancement and levels of economic development.
Natural growth rate (per thousand) = CBR − CDR.

example.q: A town has a mid-year population of 2,00,000. In the year, 4,000 babies are born and 1,600 people die. Find CBR and CDR.
steps: Natural growth rate = 20 − 8 = 12 per thousand.

learn.reallife: India's SRS data show CBR falling to about 19.5 per thousand and CDR to about 6 per thousand in recent years — signs of demographic transition.

items.q: CBR 22, CDR 7: natural growth per thousand?

games.title: Symbols and meanings
pairs: Number of deaths in the year

quiz.q: A city with a mid-year population of 5,00,000 records 12,500 live births in a year. What is its CBR (per thousand)?
steps: CBR = Bi ÷ P × 1000
Answer: 25
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by 1000 or slips a zero

quiz.q: A district of 8,00,000 people records 5,600 deaths in a year. What is its CDR (per thousand)?
steps: CDR = D ÷ P × 1000
Answer: 7
quiz.mistake: Misplaces the decimal

quiz.q: In the CBR formula, 'P' stands for:
options: Population at the end of the decade
quiz.explain: CBR uses live births in the year divided by the mid-year population.
steps: Asked: what P stands for in the CBR formula.
Lesson: CBR = (Bi ÷ P) × 1000, where P is the mid-year population.
So the answer is the mid-year population of the area.
Answer: Mid-year population of the area
quiz.mistake: Confuses P with pregnancies or density

quiz.q: Which are the three components of population change?
quiz.explain: Only births, deaths and migration change the number of people.
steps: Asked: the three components of population change.
Lesson: births, deaths and migration.
Density, sex ratio and literacy describe population but do not change its number.
Answer: Births, deaths and migration
quiz.mistake: Includes composition indicators

quiz.q: A town has CBR 28 and CDR 9 per thousand. What is its natural growth rate per thousand?
quiz.explain: Natural growth rate = CBR − CDR = 28 − 9 = 19 per thousand.
steps: Given: CBR = 28, CDR = 9 per thousand.
Natural growth rate = CBR − CDR.
28 − 9 = 19 per thousand.
Answer: 19
quiz.mistake: Adds the two rates

quiz.q: Mortality rates are affected by a region's:
options: Demographic structure, social advancement and economic development
quiz.explain: NCERT lists these three influences on death rates.
steps: Asked: what affects mortality.
Lesson: demographic structure, social advancement and level of economic development.
So the answer is those three.
Answer: Demographic structure, social advancement and economic development
quiz.mistake: Picks purely physical factors

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Crude birth rate is expressed per thousand of population. Reason (R): CBR is calculated as live births in a year divided by mid-year population, multiplied by 1000.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; multiplying by 1000 is what makes the rate 'per thousand'.
steps: Check A: CBR is per thousand — true.
Check R: CBR = (births ÷ mid-year population) × 1000 — true.
Multiplying by 1000 is what makes it 'per thousand', so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the ×1000 to 'per thousand'

quiz.q: Village X (population 4,000) had 120 births; village Y (population 10,000) had 250 births. Which has the higher CBR?
options: Y, because it had more births
steps: X: 120 ÷ 4,000 × 1000 = 30 per thousand
30 > 25, so X has the higher CBR
Answer: X (30 vs 25)
quiz.mistake: Compares raw birth numbers instead of rates

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do you calculate crude birth rate and crude death rate? What affects deaths?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Births or deaths ÷ population × 1000 — per thousand, perfect!
teach.nudge: Good! Don't forget to divide by population and multiply by 1000.

revise.summary: Births, deaths and migration change population. CBR = (live births in a year ÷ mid-year population) × 1000 and CDR = (deaths ÷ P) × 1000, both per thousand; natural growth rate = CBR − CDR.

Natural growth rate = CBR − CDR
Factors affecting mortality

Natural growth rate (per thousand) = CBR − CDR
Mortality depends on demographic structure, social advancement, economic development

Compare rates, not raw numbers of births

topics.title: Migration: types, push and pull factors

learn.hook: Every Diwali, trains from Mumbai to Patna overflow. Every harvest, Punjab's fields welcome workers from Bihar. Migration moves India.
points: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another; the place they leave is the place of origin (population falls) and the place they move to is the place of destination (population rises).
Immigrants are migrants who move into a new place; emigrants are migrants who move out of a place.
Migration may be permanent, temporary or seasonal; and rural-rural, rural-urban, urban-urban or urban-rural.
Push factors make the place of origin less attractive: unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, natural disasters, epidemics and socio-economic backwardness.
Pull factors make the destination more attractive: better job opportunities and living conditions, peace and stability, security of life and property, and pleasant climate.

example.q: A farmer from drought-hit Marathwada moves to Pune for a factory job. Identify origin, destination, a push and a pull factor.
steps: Origin: Marathwada (population falls).
Destination: Pune (population rises).
Push: drought (natural disaster) and unemployment.
Pull: better job opportunities.
example.answer: Origin Marathwada, destination Pune; push = drought/unemployment; pull = jobs

learn.reallife: Seasonal migration of sugarcane cutters from Beed to western Maharashtra and Karnataka every winter is a well-known Indian case.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a pull factor of migration?
quiz.explain: Security attracts people to a destination; the others push people out.
steps: Pull factors attract people to a destination.
Lesson list includes security of life and property.
Political turmoil, epidemics and unemployment are push factors.
Answer: Security of life and property
quiz.mistake: Confuses push and pull

quiz.q: Which of the following is a push factor?
quiz.explain: Backwardness drives people away from their place of origin.
steps: Push factors make the origin less attractive.
Lesson list includes socio-economic backwardness.
The other options are attractions at a destination, i.e. pull factors.
Answer: Socio-economic backwardness
quiz.mistake: Picks an attraction at the destination

quiz.q: Migrants who move into a new place are called:
quiz.explain: Immigrants come in; emigrants go out.
steps: Asked: name for migrants moving into a new place.
Lesson: immigrants move in; emigrants move out.
So the answer is immigrants.
Answer: Immigrants
quiz.mistake: Swaps immigrants and emigrants

quiz.q: At the place of origin, migration causes the population to:
quiz.explain: People leaving the place of origin reduce its population.
steps: Asked: effect on the place of origin.
Lesson: the place people leave loses population.
So population decreases.
Answer: Decrease
quiz.mistake: Mixes origin and destination

quiz.q: A software engineer moves from Kolkata to Bengaluru. This is which stream of migration?
quiz.explain: Both are cities, so it is urban-urban migration.
steps: Kolkata and Bengaluru are both cities.
City to city = urban-urban stream.
So the answer is urban to urban.
Answer: Urban to urban
quiz.mistake: Assumes all migration is rural-urban

quiz.q: Labourers from Bihar move to Punjab for the wheat harvest and return home after it. This is:
quiz.explain: They move for a season and return, so it is seasonal; it is mostly rural-rural.
steps: Labourers go for the harvest season and return home.
Moving for a season and returning = seasonal migration.
It is not permanent because they come back.
Answer: Seasonal migration
quiz.mistake: Thinks any long journey is permanent

quiz.q: Assertion (A): People migrate from rural to urban areas in large numbers in developing countries. Reason (R): Unemployment and poor living conditions push people out of villages, while better jobs pull them to cities.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; push and pull factors together explain rural-urban migration.
steps: Check A: large rural-urban migration in developing countries — true.
Check R: village unemployment pushes, city jobs pull — true.
Push and pull together cause the movement, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see push and pull as the explanation

quiz.q: A family leaves a flood-prone coastal village for a hill town with a cooler, safer climate. Which pair of factors is at work?
options: Push: pleasant climate; Pull: natural disaster
Push: natural disaster; Pull: pleasant climate
quiz.explain: Floods push them from the origin; the pleasant, safe climate pulls them to the destination.
steps: Floods at the origin are a natural disaster → push.
Cooler, safer climate at the destination → pull.
So Push: natural disaster; Pull: pleasant climate.
Answer: Push: natural disaster; Pull: pleasant climate
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of push and pull

teach.praise: Tweet! Push from home, pull to new places — permanent, temporary or seasonal. Clear!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you give one push factor and one pull factor, and a type of migration?

revise.summary: Migration moves people from a place of origin (population falls) to a destination (population rises). Push factors like unemployment, disasters and turmoil drive people out; pull factors like jobs, peace, security and pleasant climate draw them in.

Immigrants vs emigrants; origin vs destination
Types: permanent, temporary, seasonal; rural-urban and other streams
remember: Immigrants move into a place; emigrants move out of a place
Push: unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, disasters, epidemics, backwardness
Pull: better jobs and living conditions, peace and stability, security of life and property, pleasant climate

Not all migration is rural-urban; city to city is urban-urban

topics.title: Trends in world population growth and doubling time

learn.hook: It took more than a million years for humanity to reach 1 billion — yet only 12 years to go from 5 billion to 6 billion!
points: For most of history population grew very slowly; it was below 300 million in the first century AD.
Growth speeded up sharply after the Industrial Revolution (around 1750).
Technological advancement, expansion of world trade, better food supply and medical facilities reduced death rates, so population grew rapidly.

Doubling time — the years a population takes to double — kept shrinking: about 200 years from 1650 to 1850 (500 to 1,000 million), 80 years to 1930 (2,000 million) and 45 years to 1975 (4,000 million).
On a graph, world population looks like a 'J' curve: flat for centuries, then shooting up.

example.q: World population was 2,000 million in 1930 and 4,000 million in 1975. What was the doubling time?
steps: Doubling time = later year − earlier year when population doubled.

learn.reallife: Better food (Green Revolution), vaccines and clean water reduced deaths in India after 1951, causing a population 'explosion' between 1951 and 1981.

items.q: 5 bn to 6 bn took how many years?
Doubling time shrank from 80 to 45: by how many years?

quiz.q: World population reached 1,000 million in 1850 and 2,000 million in 1930. What was the doubling time?
steps: Given: 1,000 million in 1850, 2,000 million in 1930.
Doubling time = later year − earlier year.
Answer: 80 years
quiz.mistake: Picks the doubling time of another period

quiz.q: World population grew rapidly mainly after:
quiz.explain: Technological advances after about 1750 cut death rates and sped up growth.
steps: Asked: when growth became rapid.
Lesson: growth sped up sharply after the Industrial Revolution, around 1750.
So the answer is the Industrial Revolution.
Answer: The Industrial Revolution (around 1750)
quiz.mistake: Places rapid growth too early

quiz.q: Which factor did NOT contribute to rapid population growth after 1750?
options: Rising death rates due to famines
quiz.explain: Death rates fell, not rose; that decline drove rapid growth.
steps: Lesson: technology, trade, food supply and medical care reduced death rates.
Rising death rates from famine would slow growth, not speed it.
So 'rising death rates due to famines' did NOT contribute.
Answer: Rising death rates due to famines
quiz.mistake: Thinks famine increases population

quiz.q: How long did it take for world population to rise from 5 billion to 6 billion?
quiz.explain: NCERT notes it took only 12 years.
steps: Asked: time from 5 billion to 6 billion.
NCERT notes it took only 12 years.
So the answer is 12 years.
Answer: 12 years
quiz.mistake: Confuses this with doubling times

quiz.q: World population in the first century AD was about:
quiz.explain: It was below 300 million (0.3 billion) in the first century AD.
steps: Asked: population in the first century AD.
Lesson: it was below 300 million.
So the answer is below 300 million.
Answer: Below 300 million
quiz.mistake: Overestimates early population

quiz.q: The doubling time of world population has, over the last few centuries:
quiz.explain: From 200 to 80 to 45 years — it kept shrinking as growth sped up.
steps: Lesson doubling times: about 200 → 80 → 45 years.
The numbers keep getting smaller.
So doubling time has decreased.
Answer: Decreased
quiz.mistake: Thinks faster growth means longer doubling time

quiz.q: Assertion (A): World population growth became very rapid after the Industrial Revolution. Reason (R): Better food supply and medical facilities reduced death rates while birth rates stayed high.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; falling deaths with high births caused the rapid increase.
steps: Check A: growth became very rapid after the Industrial Revolution — true.
Check R: better food and medicine lowered deaths while births stayed high — true.
The widening gap caused fast growth, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect falling death rates to rising growth

quiz.q: If doubling time fell from 80 years to 45 years, by how many years did it shorten?
steps: Given: doubling time fell from 80 to 45 years.
Shortening = 80 − 45.
Answer: 35 years
quiz.mistake: Adds the two periods

teach.praise: Chirp-chirp! Slow, slow, then whoosh after 1750 — and doubling time keeps shrinking!
teach.nudge: Nice! Explain what doubling time means and why growth sped up after 1750.

revise.summary: World population grew very slowly for most of history (below 300 million in the first century AD) and sped up after the Industrial Revolution around 1750 as death rates fell. Doubling time shrank from about 200 to 80 to 45 years, giving a J-shaped curve.

topics.title: Spatial pattern and impact of population change

learn.hook: Japan's villages have schools with no children; Niger's schools burst at the seams. Two very different population problems.
points: Spatial pattern: developed countries generally have slow (or even negative) growth; developing countries generally grow faster. Growth is negatively correlated with economic development.
A small increase in population is desirable in a growing economy; beyond a point it creates problems.
Problems of rapid growth: depletion of resources (the most serious), unemployment, and pressure on services like schools, hospitals, housing and transport.
Population decline is also a concern: it indicates that resources that supported a former population are now insufficient; it also brings ageing and a shrinking workforce.

example.q: Compare the main population problems of a fast-growing country and a shrinking one.
steps: Fast-growing: strain on resources, jobs and services.
Shrinking: ageing, fewer workers, and a sign that resources/economy no longer support the earlier population.
Both call for planning.
example.answer: Fast growth strains resources; decline brings ageing and shrinking workforce

learn.reallife: Indian cities like Bengaluru face traffic, water and housing stress from rapid growth, while states like Kerala are already planning for an ageing population.

Richer countries generally grow more slowly.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the spatial pattern of population growth?
options: Developed countries grow slowly; developing countries grow faster
Developed countries grow faster than developing ones
All countries grow at the same rate

Growth is negatively correlated with development.

quiz.q: Which is described as the most serious problem of rapid population growth?
quiz.explain: Fast growth uses up resources faster than they can be replaced.

Lesson: depletion of resources.
Ageing and a shrinking workforce are problems of decline.
Answer: Depletion of resources

quiz.q: A small increase in population is considered:

Lesson: it is desirable in a growing economy; problems come beyond a point.
So the answer is desirable in a growing economy.
Answer: Desirable in a growing economy
quiz.mistake: Thinks every increase is bad

quiz.q: Which of these is a concern of population decline?
quiz.explain: Fewer births mean fewer young workers and more elderly.
steps: Asked: a concern of population decline.
Lesson: decline brings ageing and a shrinking workforce.
Overcrowded schools and too many jobseekers go with rapid growth.
Answer: Ageing and a shrinking workforce

quiz.q: Population growth and economic development are generally:
quiz.explain: As development rises, growth tends to fall.
steps: Lesson: as development rises, growth tends to fall.
When one rises and the other falls, they are negatively correlated.
So the answer is negatively correlated.
Answer: Negatively correlated
quiz.mistake: Thinks rich countries have more children

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Population decline is a matter of concern. Reason (R): It indicates that resources that supported a former population are now insufficient to maintain it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; NCERT explains the concern this way.
steps: Check A: population decline is a concern — true.
Check R: resources that supported the former population are now insufficient — true.
That is exactly why decline worries planners, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks only population growth is a concern

quiz.q: A city's population doubles in 20 years while water supply stays the same. Water available per person will:
quiz.explain: Same water shared by twice the people gives half per person.
steps: Water per person = total water ÷ population.
Water same, population × 2.
Share = water ÷ (2 × population) = half of before, so it halves.
Answer: Halve
quiz.mistake: Thinks more people means more water

quiz.q: Which pair is correct?
options: Rapid growth — ageing; Decline — unemployment from too many youths

steps: Rapid growth brings unemployment and strain on services.
Decline brings ageing.
So 'Rapid growth — unemployment; Decline — ageing' is correct.
Answer: Rapid growth — unemployment; Decline — ageing
quiz.mistake: Swaps the effects

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is population growth good or bad? What problems come from growing too fast or shrinking?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A little growth helps, too much drains resources, and decline means ageing. Balanced view!
teach.nudge: Good! Mention problems of both rapid growth and population decline.

revise.summary: Developed countries generally grow slowly and developing countries faster, so growth is negatively correlated with development. Rapid growth depletes resources and strains jobs and services, while decline brings ageing and a shrinking workforce.

Problems of rapid growth vs problems of decline
Per-person share when population rises and resources stay fixed
remember: Population growth is negatively correlated with economic development
Most serious problem of rapid growth: depletion of resources
A small increase is desirable in a growing economy
Decline: ageing, shrinking workforce; resources no longer sufficient for the former population

learn.hook: Two hundred years ago, every country had high births and high deaths. Today some have cradles empty and pensions full. The demographic transition explains the journey.
points: Demographic transition theory: population changes from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths as society moves from rural, agrarian and illiterate to urban, industrial and literate. It helps describe and predict population.

Stage I: high fertility and high mortality, so slow growth; people mostly in agriculture, large families, low life expectancy, mostly illiterate, low technology. About 200 years ago all countries were in this stage.
Stage II: fertility remains high at first and declines with time; mortality falls due to better sanitation and health — the gap between births and deaths causes a large increase in population.
Stage III: both fertility and mortality decline considerably; population is stable or grows slowly; society is urbanised, literate, with high technical know-how and deliberately controls family size.

On the diagram, the birth-rate and death-rate curves start high, the death-rate curve falls first, the birth-rate curve falls later; total population rises steeply in the gap. Countries today are at different stages.

example.q: A country has a birth rate of 38 and a death rate of 12 per thousand, with death rates falling fast due to new hospitals. Which stage is it in?
steps: High birth rate still (38).
Death rate already falling (12).
Large gap → rapid growth.
This matches Stage II.

learn.reallife: India moved from Stage II (high births, falling deaths after 1951) towards Stage III, with total fertility rate now at about 2.0 (NFHS-5) — below replacement level.

games.title: Through the transition

quiz.q: According to demographic transition theory, population changes from:
options: High births and high deaths to low births and low deaths
Low births and low deaths to high births and high deaths
High births and low deaths to high deaths
quiz.explain: As societies modernise, both rates fall from high to low.
steps: Lesson: population moves from high births and deaths to low births and deaths.
This happens as society becomes urban, industrial and literate.
The reversed option has the direction backwards.
Answer: High births and high deaths to low births and low deaths
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction

quiz.q: In which stage does population increase the most rapidly?
options: Growth is equal in all stages
quiz.explain: Deaths fall while births remain high, so the gap is widest in Stage II.
steps: In Stage II deaths fall but births stay high.
The gap between births and deaths is widest then.
So population rises fastest in Stage II.
Answer: Stage II
quiz.mistake: Picks Stage I because births are highest

quiz.q: Stage I of demographic transition is characterised by:
options: High fertility, high mortality and slow growth
quiz.explain: In Stage I both rates are high and cancel out, so growth is slow.
steps: Lesson: Stage I has high fertility and high mortality.
High deaths cancel high births.
So growth is slow — high fertility, high mortality, slow growth.
Answer: High fertility, high mortality and slow growth
quiz.mistake: Thinks high births always mean fast growth

quiz.q: What mainly causes mortality to decline in Stage II?
options: Urban industrial lifestyle reducing family size
Improvements in sanitation and health conditions
quiz.explain: Better sanitation and health reduce death rates.
steps: Asked: why mortality falls in Stage II.
Lesson: better sanitation and health conditions.
Smaller families explain falling births later, not falling deaths.
Answer: Improvements in sanitation and health conditions
quiz.mistake: Confuses causes of falling deaths with falling births

quiz.q: A society that is urbanised, literate and deliberately limits family size is in:
quiz.explain: These are features of Stage III.
steps: Urbanised, literate, deliberately limiting family size.
Lesson: these are features of Stage III.
So the answer is Stage III.
Answer: Stage III
quiz.mistake: Picks Stage II

quiz.q: On a demographic transition diagram, which curve falls first?
options: Both fall together at the start
quiz.explain: Death rate drops first (Stage II); birth rate falls later.
steps: Lesson: the death-rate curve falls first; the birth-rate curve falls later.
That is why Stage II grows fast.
So the answer is death rate.
Answer: Death rate
quiz.mistake: Thinks births fall before deaths

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Population grows slowly in Stage III. Reason (R): Both fertility and mortality have declined considerably.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; with both rates low, the gap is small and growth slow.
steps: Check A: growth is slow in Stage III — true.
Check R: both fertility and mortality have declined considerably — true.
With both low, the gap is small, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks low death rate always means fast growth

quiz.q: A country has CBR 15 and CDR 8 per thousand, high literacy and mostly urban living. Its natural growth rate and likely stage are:
quiz.explain: 15 − 8 = 7 per thousand; low rates with urban literate society indicate Stage III.
steps: Natural growth rate = CBR − CDR = 15 − 8 = 7 per thousand
Low birth and death rates with an urban, literate society → Stage III
Answer: 7 per thousand; Stage III
quiz.mistake: Adds the rates or misreads the stage

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Explain the demographic transition theory and its three stages.'
teach.praise: Chirp-chirp! High-high, then deaths drop, then low-low. That's the transition!
teach.nudge: Good! Describe what happens to birth and death rates in each of the three stages.

revise.summary: Demographic transition theory says population moves from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths as society becomes urban, industrial and literate. Growth is slow in Stage I, fastest in Stage II (deaths fall first), and slow again in Stage III.
focus: Features of Stages I, II and III
Why the gap in Stage II causes rapid growth
Reading the diagram: death rate falls first
remember: Stage I: high fertility, high mortality, slow growth; agrarian, illiterate, low technology
Stage II: fertility high then declining; mortality falls (sanitation, health) → large increase
Stage III: both low; slow or stable growth; urban, literate, family size controlled
traps: High births alone do not mean fast growth — in Stage I high deaths cancel them
The birth-rate curve does not fall first; the death rate falls first

learn.hook: In 1798 an English clergyman predicted that people would outgrow food and face famine. Was Thomas Malthus right?
points: Family planning is the spacing or preventing of the birth of children; access to family planning services helps limit population growth and improves women's health.
Government measures include propaganda (awareness campaigns), free availability of contraceptives and tax disincentives for large families.
Thomas Malthus (1798): the number of people would increase faster than the food supply; any further increase would result in a population crash caused by famine, disease and war.
Malthus' natural (physical) checks are famine, disease and war; preventive checks (like late marriage and self-restraint) are better than physical checks.
Exam focus: distribution factors, positive vs negative growth, CBR/CDR numericals and stages of demographic transition.

example.q: Classify Malthus' checks: delayed marriage, famine, epidemic, self-restraint, war.
steps: Natural/physical checks occur through suffering: famine, epidemic (disease), war.
Preventive checks are chosen by people: delayed marriage, self-restraint.
example.answer: Natural checks: famine, epidemic, war; preventive checks: delayed marriage, self-restraint

learn.reallife: India launched the world's first national family planning programme in 1952; schemes like Mission Parivar Vikas promote access to contraceptives in high-fertility districts.
